articles.title: Workplace absenteeism: Why temporary disability is a right, not an expense
articles.dek: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .
paragraphs: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .

Temporary disability is a cornerstone of the public Social Security system. It is a right for all workers who fall ill and a social security benefit designed primarily to protect those who are sick, enabling them to receive medical treatment and recover or improve their condition while ensuring they have sufficient income during periods in which they are unable to work.

In 2025, nearly 6 million such episodes were recorded in Spain. In an open-access article published in the journal Labos , Miguel Arenas Gómez, a researcher at the UOC-DIGIT center and lecturer in the Faculty of Law and Political Science at the Universitat Oberta de Catalunya (UOC), analyzes the stigma surrounding this benefit, which is considered an expense when examined from a macroeconomic perspective.

"This opinion piece challenges the institutional narrative put forward by the Independent Authority for Fiscal Responsibility (AIReF), which advocates tightening access to the benefit and reducing financial support as a way of controlling public spending," argues Arenas, a member of the Taxation, Labor Relations and Business Research Group (TAXBUSINESS).
Based on statistical analysis and legislative reforms to the benefit in recent years, the article contends that the debate should focus on issues that extend beyond the economic realm.

"The very actors driving the debate are also implicitly stigmatizing workers by unjustifiably associating sick leave with fraud, moral laxity or individual opportunism," explains the lecturer and labor law expert. "Absences from work that are medically justified are being portrayed as irregular, diverting attention from the real reasons for sick leave," he adds.

According to the article, absences caused by temporary disability are not a matter of employees simply choosing not to work. Rather, they are linked to structural factors such as an aging workforce, long health care waiting lists and the incidence of psychosocial risks.
The progressive and accelerated aging of the workforce is one of the factors having the greatest impact on this benefit.

"Expecting an increasingly older workforce to maintain the same rates of workplace accidents and illness as two decades ago is mathematically unrealistic. Bodies age and chronic conditions become more prevalent; therefore, the spike in cases of temporary disability isn't a sign of fraud, but an accurate reflection of a demographic reality that the labor market must acknowledge," the article notes.
This trend is compounded by the fact that people are retiring at an older age.

Second, the length of sick leave is linked to the "structural collapse" of primary care services and waiting lists for specialist appointments within Spain's National Health System. This situation is further exacerbated by a surge in psychosocial risks and neurological conditions in an increasingly digitalized working environment.

"Technostress, techno-invasion, digital fatigue resulting from the inability to effectively disconnect from work and burnout have become some of the real but often invisible causes of medical leave," Arenas points out.

Another important factor is gender differences in relation to temporary disability. In 2025, women accounted for more than 3. 1 million new cases of sick leave, compared with just over 2. 6 million among men. However, this higher incidence does not translate into longer periods of leave, but rather shorter ones. The average duration of sick leave was 37 days for women, compared with 40. 3 days for men.

According to the article, these figures suggest that workers in precarious jobs or roles involving intense physical or psychological demands are more likely to fall ill, and to do so repeatedly. These sectors include occupations that are largely dominated by women, including health care, education, social services and care work.

articles.title: New light-conversion tool could help speed up quantum computing

paragraphs: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .
Want to break down some basics in the world of quantum research over dinner? Researchers at the Cockrell School of Engineering have you covered.

In a collaboration with seven other institutions, UT engineers have developed a new tool to advance the speed of processing in quantum computing. Quantum computers use physics concepts to process information beyond the traditional computer's binary. By analyzing "quantum bits," or basic units of information that exploit superposition and interference, quantum computers are capable of problem-solving at incredible speeds. The solution to achieving even quicker speeds, which involves stacked ultrathin layers of semiconductor materials, lies in controlling the color of light.

The technology, which the team called "asymmetric coupled quantum wells," proved over seven times as effective as other materials in the pursuit of light conversion. Light is significant to matters of quantum because the speed of light can determine the speed of the photons that carry and process information. The team's findings are published in the journal Optica .

While light speed itself is consistent when traveling in a vacuum, the introduction of different materials alters light's speed and wavelength. Understanding—and therefore harnessing—the light allows researchers to gain more control over computing processes and even device size.

Having a grasp on the thickness or qualities of different materials is promising for quantum to grow in scale, and with that, researchers can also "tune" the materials to suit the needs of other technologies.

articles.title: AI has solved a host of big math problems—here's why this threatens the whole field of mathematics
articles.dek: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .
paragraphs: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .

For many, the year 2026 will be remembered as the one when mathematics had an identity crisis and forever changed. Frontier (cutting-edge) AI models made by OpenAI and Anthropic made stunning progress on hundreds of open problems that have baffled mathematicians for decades—and centuries in some cases.

From April this year, a steady stream of impressive AI-discovered results emerged. It started with a breakthrough by OpenAI on the Erdős unit distance conjecture and the Jacobian conjecture, both of which had been unsolved for decades.

Then, in September and October, two stunning announcements were made. First, OpenAI announced a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem —one of the seven "millennium problems" highlighted by the Clay Mathematics Institute in the year 2000. Second, OpenAI released a trove of over 700 papers claiming solutions, proofs or counterexamples (which show that a claim or conjecture is false) to 372 open problems that are at the forefront of mathematics research.

Now, Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge has announced a Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis . This is arguably the most famous problem in mathematics, proposed by the German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1867.

The October "OpenAI dump," as it has become known, sent shock waves through the mathematics community because of its sheer scale. Hugo Duminil-Copin, professor and Fields medalist (the medal is a top accolade in mathematics), from the Institute of Advanced Scientific Studies in Paris, said the dump had " annihilated my field of research ." He also warned that it could "dismantle" the discipline of mathematics.

Tech companies were able to make such staggering progress on difficult problems because, first, their specific AI technology, called large language models (LLMs), is trained on the entire human corpus of mathematical literature (and much more).

Second, the companies created " AI agents ," software systems built around the LLM that extend its capabilities to reasoning, taking actions and executing code. Agents can also observe the results of their actions, taking further action if required.

For the solution to the Navier-Stokes equation, OpenAI set 10,000 AI agents to work collaboratively. It took 88 hours for these agents to find their solution. A further 17 hours was needed to have the solution verified through formalization and verification software called Lean .

Alpöge's Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis runs to more than 250,000 pages. The Lean code verification is over 17 million lines long . His Lean proof has since been verified by independent researchers .

Unlike the Poincaré conjecture , a millennium problem solved by the Russian mathematician Grigori Perelman in the early 2000s, the Navier-Stokes equation (like all the other 300+ problems in the OpenAI dump) was resolved by AI agents with almost no human intervention.

This is truly extraordinary. A metaphor illustrating how these agents work might be a colony of Australian cathedral termites . Each insect in the colony mindlessly does its local thing, but in concert, the termites build impressive castles, often more than 6 meters (20 feet) high, replete with ventilation, a form of air conditioning and weather protection.
Likewise, each AI agent chips away at its local task, but collectively, these swarms of agents can now solve—and verify—the hardest known math problems.

articles.title: Do a violin's physical characteristics really improve with regular playing?
articles.dek: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .
paragraphs: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .

There is a widespread notion among violinists: A violin "opens up" as it is played, which is to say its sound gradually improves. However, an experiment conducted by a team led by a CNRS researcher has challenged this belief in a study published in Acta Acustica . After six months, the professional soloist in charge of playing the violin judged the process complete, reporting that the instrument had become easier to play and its tone had improved. Yet, no physical or acoustic measurement confirmed that this feeling resulted from such a mechanical change in the instrument itself.

To achieve these results, the team asked the violinist to play an instrument rarely used before the experiment on a daily basis. Two other violins, also little-played but in storage throughout the experiment, served as control instruments. By comparing the physical characteristics and acoustic signatures of the three instruments before and after six months of use, the scientists were unable to identify any significant improvement in the instrument played by the musician, despite her evolving perception.

These results were reaffirmed by the evaluations of other violinists, who were invited to make a blind comparison of the tone and power of the three instruments, as well as those of 30 listeners who listened to excerpts recorded at the beginning and end of the study. What is more, the comparison of the soloist's gestures before and after showed no adaptation on her part in terms of playing technique.

These results suggest that the impression that a violin "opens up" could result more from the musician's cognitive adaptation with practice than from a physical transformation of the instrument or a gestural adaptation. As the violinist becomes more familiar with its acoustic and mechanical qualities, their sensations change, and the violin can seem easier to play. The study invites us to reexamine this firmly established belief in the musical world.

Blind evaluations likewise detected no improvement, despite the player's reports of better tone and playability. These results do not support a measurable mechanical basis for the violin “opening up.”

articles.title: Genetic mosaic helps explain diverse forms of Darwin's finches
articles.dek: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .
paragraphs: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .

Darwin's finches are known for their varied beaks, which help them take advantage of different food sources in the Galápagos Islands. Much previous research has focused on seed-eating ground finches, but their relatives that search for insects in forested areas have received less attention.

Now, research from the Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences (VMBS) and international collaborators reveals that some of these tree finches are closer relatives than their distinctly different beaks suggest.

Although western large tree finches look like other large tree finches, researchers found that most of their DNA more closely resembles that of small tree finches. One important exception is a region associated with beak and body size, which resembles that of large tree finches.

Scientists call this mixture of genetic material from different ancestral lineages a "genetic mosaic." The finding suggests that interbreeding can help produce new combinations of traits, allowing birds to differ in how they look and feed even when most of their DNA is very similar.
The findings, published in Nature Communications , offer insight into how interbreeding and natural selection can work together to shape diversity.

"Species or populations with mosaic genomes are more common than we previously thought and such gene flow between species can be very important for adaptation," said Dr. Leif Andersson, a professor in VMBS' Department of Veterinary Integrative Biosciences.

Andersson pointed to his team's earlier research on Baltic herring , which found that genetic variants acquired from Pacific herring helped the fish adapt to the Baltic Sea's low-salinity water. Such exchanges can give populations useful genetic variation for surviving in different environments.

The international team combined whole-genome sequences from hundreds of birds with measurements from museum specimens. Combining the two sources allowed researchers to test whether similarities in physical appearance, or phenotype, reflected close evolutionary relationships.
"Two birds can be very similar on the phenotypic level but show striking genetic differences and vice versa," Andersson said.

Among the most striking examples were small tree finches and western large tree finches living on the same islands. Despite their close genetic relationship, differences in beak and body size help them use different food resources.

Researchers already knew that G03, a supergene associated with beak and body size, influences these traits in Darwin's finches. This study revealed that it accounts for one of the main genetic differences between small tree finches and western large tree finches.
"A supergene is a cluster of genes that are inherited as a block that often affect more than one trait, because different genes within the supergene affect different traits," Andersson said.
The mosaic pattern appeared in western large tree finches on Isabela and Fernandina islands.

articles.title: Recipe for one of the world's most important cancer drugs uncovered: Tobacco plants could produce the medicine
articles.dek: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .
paragraphs: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .

More people around the world will receive a cancer diagnosis at some point in their lives. As this trend is expected to continue, researchers have been working to crack the code of how the widely used cancer drug Taxol (paclitaxel) is naturally produced, with the aim of making its production cheaper and more efficient in the future.

Today, Taxol, which is used to treat breast cancer, ovarian cancer and lung cancer, is produced through a long process that extracts related plant compounds from plants and converts them to the drug through a series of complex chemical reactions. This makes Taxol one of the most expensive medicines available.

"That is why it has been essential to understand how Taxol can be produced biosynthetically, so that treatment can become more accessible to patients around the world," says professor Sotirios Kampranis from the Department of Plant and Environmental Sciences, who is also the senior author of the study published in Nature Chemical Biology .

Taxol originally comes from the yew tree, where the active compound is produced in the bark. Although Taxol has long been produced for cancer treatment, there has never been a complete manual describing the process that the plants use to make it. Now, researchers have assembled that missing guide.

"We have tested numerous hypotheses to uncover the complete biological pathway for producing Taxol from start to finish. We now have a blueprint, essentially a recipe, that can be used to produce Taxol in plants, yeast or other systems. This could pave the way for new methods of producing Taxol that make manufacturing easier and the final product more affordable," says Kampranis.

In the study, the researchers took candidate genes responsible for Taxol production from the yew tree and introduced them into another plant, the tobacco species Nicotiana benthamiana. This plant grows quickly and is widely used in research.

"We introduced more than 20 of the yew tree genes into tobacco plants to demonstrate the entire biological process of Taxol production step by step," says Zhen Fan, a postdoctoral researcher at the Department of Plant and Environmental Sciences and co-first author of the study.
The researchers succeeded in getting the tobacco plants to produce Taxol at levels comparable to those found naturally in yew tree bark.
"The tobacco plant is an effective platform for growing Taxol because it provides the same cellular environment as the yew tree but is a lot faster to grow and easier to engineer," says Kampranis.
For tobacco plants to be used in large-scale production in the future, the yew tree genes will need to become a stable part of the plant's own genetic makeup.

"That is the next major challenge. Large-scale production, for example in greenhouses, requires stable plants that permanently contain the yew genes, so that we do not have to introduce them every time," says Kampranis.
In addition to using tobacco plants to produce the cancer drug, the researchers point to other possible production methods.

"Now that we have the crucial blueprint for biosynthetic Taxol production, there is potential to produce it in many different ways. We also see fermented yeast cells as a promising solution," says Kampranis.

articles.title: This 3D-Printed Robot Runs, Swims, and Climbs Without Any Electronics
articles.dek: A robot powered entirely by air could offer a new way to explore dangerous environments where radiation or strong magnetic fields threaten conventional electronics.
paragraphs: A robot powered entirely by air could offer a new way to explore dangerous environments where radiation or strong magnetic fields threaten conventional electronics.
A six-legged robot made entirely of soft materials can run at speeds of up to 10. 6 miles per hour (4. 72 meters per second), making it the fastest soft robot of its kind.

Built by engineers at the University of California, San Diego , the machine can race across sand, gravel, and concrete, run down stairs, and even swim. Perhaps most remarkably, the entire robot is 3D-printed in one piece using a single material, and it needs no electronics to move.

The breakthrough, described in Science Robotics , takes inspiration from a centuries-old invention, the steam engine. By adapting the way steam engines make efficient use of pressure, researchers found a way to make their soft robot run more than 100 times faster than an earlier version.

The project began with a much slower machine. In 2022, researchers at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering developed a 3D-printed, air-powered robot that could walk at just 4 centimeters (about 1. 6 inches) per second. Described in a 2025 paper in Advanced Intelligent Systems , the original design demonstrated that a robot could move using nothing more than a network of air-filled chambers and valves built directly into its soft body. Its speed, however, was limited by how much air pressure and airflow the internal structures could withstand.

“Our first walking robot demonstrated what was possible, but it was too slow. We hoped to overcome this limitation, and we were fortunate to find a solution to make the new robot 100 times faster,” said Yichen Zhai, a former postdoctoral researcher in Professor Michael T. Tolley’s Bioinspired Robotics and Design Laboratory at UC San Diego.

Zhai and Tolley’s team knew that increasing the air pressure could make the robot move faster. Inside the machine, a connected network of chambers, valves, and tubes directs compressed air to move its legs. Making those structures larger and stronger would allow more air to flow through at higher pressures, but there was a catch. At high speeds, the robot could exhaust pressurized air before using much of its remaining energy, wasting the very power needed to keep it running.

The researchers found their solution in the compound steam engine, which extracts more useful energy by allowing steam to expand through multiple chambers rather than releasing it all at once. They incorporated a similar arrangement into the robot, giving compressed air two jobs as it moves through the body. First, it passes through smaller, high-pressure chambers to operate the valves. It then travels into larger, low-pressure chambers, where it drives the legs.

This two-stage system allows the robot to make better use of its compressed air while achieving speeds far beyond those of its predecessor. It also preserves one of the design’s most appealing features: the entire network of moving parts can be printed together without requiring separate electronic controls.

The researchers described the engineering challenge this way, “The key challenge was to implement a time-tested solution (the compound steam engine) in a soft running robot that can be printed in a single piece out of a single material. We see this as a step towards complex and powerful robots that can be printed on the desktop using inexpensive materials.”

To see what their creation could handle, the team tested it across concrete, gravel, lawns, mulch, and sand. The robot successfully navigated these different surfaces, ran down stairs, swam in water, and continued functioning underwater. Its ability to move through such varied environments demonstrates what can be accomplished with a relatively simple, flexible design powered entirely by air.

There is still one major limitation. Although the robot operates without electronics, it remains tethered to an external source of compressed air, such as a conventional air compressor. The researchers hope to reduce its air consumption enough that future versions could carry a portable supply, potentially using a small cartridge of compressed air instead. They also want to develop more sophisticated movements that would allow the robot to steer and manipulate objects.

articles.title: Researchers Just Sent an Unblockable Message Through a Solid Wall Using Gravity
articles.dek: Researchers have demonstrated an unusual way to transmit information through solid barriers using gravity rather than electromagnetic signals.
paragraphs: Researchers have demonstrated an unusual way to transmit information through solid barriers using gravity rather than electromagnetic signals.

Physicists at the University of Queensland have transmitted a message through a brick wall using gravity instead of electromagnetic signals. Their unconventional communication system relied on a moving elevator counterweight and an extremely sensitive instrument capable of detecting tiny changes in the gravitational field.

The experiment took place in UQ’s Parnell Building, where researchers moved a 1. 8-metric-ton (about 4,000 pounds) elevator counterweight between two positions representing binary 0 and 1. A gravimeter positioned in a nearby bathroom detected the gravitational changes and decoded a single word: “Gravity.”

Unlike radio waves and other electromagnetic signals, gravitational fields cannot be blocked by ordinary building materials. This means information carried by changes in gravity could potentially reach places where conventional wireless communication struggles.

Dr. Charles Woffinden from UQ’s School of Mathematics and Physics explained the advantage. “Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” he said. “Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with Wi-Fi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.”
“While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block.”

The communication experiment grew out of an unrelated effort to measure vehicle weights without physical contact. Dr. Andrew Groszek and his colleagues were developing a system that could estimate the mass of trucks and other heavy vehicles by detecting their gravitational attraction.

“We were aiming to determine the mass of trucks and other large vehicles by measuring their tiny gravitational pull,” Dr. Groszek said. “Once we had shown that the idea worked, we realized the same physics could be used to encode and transmit information.”

The researchers applied that principle to communication by moving a large mass between fixed positions. Each movement altered the gravitational field measured by the detector, allowing the team to encode binary information without transmitting electromagnetic signals.
Although the experiment successfully transmitted information, its data rate was exceptionally low. Professor Andrew White identified the aging elevator as a major constraint.
“Our lift was snail-paced – it’s from the 1950s – so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word,” Professor White said.
“The speed of gravity communication would come down to how big the mass is, how fast you can move it, and the sensitivity of the detector.”
“It took more than 100 years to go from the first telegraph system to the mobile phone, so while gravity communication is not practical today, it could be in the future.”

Professor Matthew Davis said the experiment established that information can be deliberately encoded in a gravitational field and recovered by a detector. The achievement demonstrates the underlying physics, although substantial improvements would be needed before the technique could serve as a useful communication system.

articles.title: NATO witnesses a surge of airspace violations by Russia as Moscow seeks to test alliance
articles.dek: NATO convened an urgent meeting on Nov. 23, 2026 , to discuss the violation of members’ airspace by Russia.
paragraphs: NATO convened an urgent meeting on Nov. 23, 2026 , to discuss the violation of members’ airspace by Russia.

It follows an incident three days earlier in which three objects – believed to be two missiles and a drone – crashed in Poland in what the country’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, described as an “intentional provocation” by Russia . If true, it would be far from the first such testing of the airspace of a NATO country.

Russian aircraft, drones and missiles have violated NATO airspace dozens of times since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. And while individually, many of these incidents appear minor – a drone crash here, a brief fighter incursion there, a missile discovered only after the fact – taken together, I believe the numbers tell a far more troubling story.
To get a full picture of the scale of violations, I conducted a systematic review of Russian airspace violations against NATO members ) from 2022 through the end of November.

It reveals not just an increase but a sharp acceleration accompanied by rising severity and widening geographic scope. In 2026, through Nov. 20, NATO members recorded 25 attributed Russian airspace violations – more than four times as many as in 2024 and 43% of all incidents recorded over the five-year period.
This has not been a gradual escalation; it was a dramatic change.

I identified airspace violations through a systematic review of international news media coverage, corroborated with official NATO press releases and cross-validated against operational assessments and geospatial reporting from the Institute for the Study of War .
Included were violations of airspace by drones heavily suspected to be Russian but that could not be 100% confirmed.

Between 2022 and 2024, the annual number of violations rose steadily but modestly. There were four incidents in 2022, five in 2023 and six in 2024. That corresponds to year-on-year increases of roughly 25% and 20%.
In 2025, the count jumped to 18, a 200% increase in a single year. And that pace has continued into 2026.

Such a surge is statistically and strategically significant. It strongly suggests that Russian airspace violations are no longer episodic spillovers from the war in Ukraine, but part of a sustained pattern of pressure directed at NATO itself. The 2026 figures reinforce this: The count has kept rising even after the 2025 surge.

In 2022, all four violations were what I classify as low-intensity events: brief incursions into Swedish airspace by Russian fighters, the crash of an Orlan-10 reconnaissance drone in Romania and the later discovery of a Russian cruise missile in Poland. These incidents were serious but short-lived and geographically limited.

By 2023, violations had become more repetitive. Romania alone experienced multiple drone incursions and debris discoveries over several months, often triggering fighter scrambles. All five incidents that year fell into a midrange severity category: more persistent than before but still largely confined to border regions.

The transition toward higher-intensity incursions became clearer in 2024. Of the six violations that year, half involved high-severity characteristics such as deeper penetration of a NATO country or broader geographic exposure. A Russian cruise missile crossed into Polish airspace , drones entered Romania on multiple consecutive nights, and a Russian drone crashed well inside Latvian territory . These incidents expanded both the depth and the geographic footprint of violations.

Then came 2025. Of the 18 violations recorded that year , a clear majority qualify as high-severity events. These include a Russian drone that penetrated nearly 60 miles (100 kilometers) into Polish territory before crashing near Osiny without prior radar detection; a drone that remained inside Romanian airspace for approximately four hours, crossing multiple counties before crashing in Vaslui; and a massive 21-drone swarm over Poland on Sept. 9-10 that forced the closure of major civilian airports in Warsaw, Rzeszów and Lublin.

Manned aircraft also returned in force. Russian MiG-31 interceptors flew over Estonia for about 12 minutes with transponders – onboard devices that automatically respond to radar signals by transmitting an aircraft’s identity and altitude, enabling air traffic control and air defense systems to track it – switched off.
In October, a Russian Su-30 fighter accompanied by an Il-78 refueling tanker violated Lithuanian airspace – an unmistakable signal of endurance and deliberate mission planning.
In December 2025, suspected Russian drones were shot down and later recovered in Turkey on multiple dates, indicating a persistent provocation rather than a one-off incursion.

Perhaps most strikingly, Western Europe was seemingly no longer exempt. On Dec. 4, 2025, five unidentified drones flew over France’s Île Longue naval base , home to the country’s nuclear ballistic missile submarines. French personnel reportedly fired at the suspected Russian drones.
Just weeks later, on Christmas Day, Polish fighters intercepted a Russian reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea.

In 2026, the incidents grew more dangerous. In May, a Russian drone struck an apartment block in Galați, Romania , injuring two people, the first civilian injuries on NATO soil from such an incursion. Then on July 30, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile flew roughly 60 miles (100 kilometers) into Poland before exploding in a field near Lublin. On Nov. 20, during a mass Russian strike on Ukraine, a Kh-101, likely a second missile and a jet-powered drone entered Polish airspace .

Manned aircraft also crossed into NATO airspace. A Russian Su-30 fighter entered Estonian airspace in March with no flight plan and no contact with air traffic control, and in September, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter crossed from Kaliningrad into Poland .

Severity and frequency are not the only dimensions that changed. Geographical reach has, too. In 2022, Russian violations affected three NATO members. By 2024, that number had grown to four. In 2025, it expanded to six: Romania, Poland, Estonia, Lithuania, Turkey and France. In 2026, the violations attributed to Russia have so far been concentrated in four members – Romania, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania – with Romania alone accounting for 20 of the 25. Romania’s defense ministry counted 35 unauthorized drone entries by mid-October, many too brief to be reported individually.
Pressure was applied simultaneously in the Black Sea region, the Baltic states and Western Europe.

articles.title: NASA Awards Contract for NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network Program
articles.dek: NASA, on behalf of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), has awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation for the Sounder for…
paragraphs: NASA, on behalf of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), has awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation for the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) instruments on NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) satellites.

The cost-plus-fixed-fee, firm-fixed-price, and time-and-materials hybrid contract has a value of $290. 6 million. The period of performance runs from Nov. 23 through April 1, 2042. The work will take place at the awardee’s facility.

Under the contract, Northrop Grumman will provide the design, development, production, testing, and mission support for three SMBA instruments, the next generation of low Earth orbit microwave sounders. NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, is managing the acquisition, and NOAA will own and operate the instruments and deliver the data to users worldwide. Microwave sounders provide critical measurements of temperature and moisture in the atmosphere, which significantly influence weather patterns. The SMBA instruments could improve the medium-range forecasts for NOAA’s National Weather Service.

The NEON mission is a collaboration between NASA and NOAA. The mission is led by NOAA, which provides funding, technical requirements, and postlaunch operations. NASA will manage the development of the NEON satellites and launch them for NOAA. NASA and NOAA will work with commercial partners to design and build the NEON spacecraft and instruments.

NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, is managing the acquisition, and NOAA will own and operate the instruments and deliver the data to users worldwide. Microwave sounders provide critical measurements of temperature and moisture in the atmosphere, which significantly influence weather patterns. The SMBA instruments could improve the medium-range forecasts for NOAA’s National Weather Service.

The NEON mission is a collaboration between NASA and NOAA. The mission is led by NOAA, which provides funding, technical requirements, and postlaunch operations. NASA will manage the development of the NEON satellites and launch them for NOAA. NASA and NOAA will work with commercial partners to design and build the NEON spacecraft and instruments.

articles.title: A 360-Year-Old Manuscript Reveals Galileo May Have Built a Telescope Far Ahead of Its Time
articles.dek: Galileo left no technical analyses of his telescopes, but a centuries-old manuscript may offer the clearest look yet at a more sophisticated instrument he could have built.
paragraphs: Galileo left no technical analyses of his telescopes, but a centuries-old manuscript may offer the clearest look yet at a more sophisticated instrument he could have built.

In 1666, a Spanish friar hoping to secure his passage home was given an unusual test of his scientific abilities. A powerful colonial official handed him a telescope and demanded a detailed explanation of how it worked. Nearly 360 years later, the account he produced has resurfaced with a remarkable claim: the instrument was made by Galileo Galilei, and its design may be far more advanced than historians previously believed possible for his time.

The account was discovered by Dr. José María Moreno Madrid, a researcher at the University of Limerick’s School of History and Geography in Ireland, while examining a manuscript written by Dominican friar Ignacio Muñoz. Dated 1666 and titled De Tellescopiis Stellarum , the document describes a four-lens telescope that Muñoz identified with the Latin phrase “fabricatum a Galilaeo,” meaning “manufactured by Galileo.”

The description is unusually precise. Muñoz documented the telescope’s individual components, including its reverse-tapered body and an arrangement of four lenses that allowed distant objects to appear upright. His account describes an erecting eyepiece and convex lenses separated by twice their focal lengths, accompanied by detailed diagrams and drawings that show how the instrument was constructed.

These technical details matter because historical records have generally placed the earliest four-lens telescopes around 1643 to 1645, with their production becoming widespread across Europe beginning in the 1640s. If the instrument really came from Galileo’s workshop, the timeline of telescope development would need to be reconsidered.
In research published in Annals of Science , Moreno Madrid explains what the attribution could mean.

“If, as the text claims, the telescope analyzed was indeed manufactured by Galileo, then the earliest known experimentation with four-lens telescopes would have to be pushed back to 1630 at the latest and credited to him. Moreover, Muñoz’s De Tellescopiis Stellarum would become the most detailed technical analysis of a telescope provenly made by Galileo – and, somewhat paradoxically, it would concern a four-lens telescope rather than the Galilean design that ultimately came to bear his name,” said Dr. Moreno Madrid.

The circumstances surrounding Muñoz’s examination provide another intriguing piece of the story. After traveling from Spain to the Philippines, he became involved in an illicit attempt to establish a new Dominican religious order and was subsequently exiled to Portuguese India. Hoping to return to Spain, he contacted King Philip IV with a proposal that promised to improve the performance of Spanish fleets operating around the world.

Muñoz offered his nautical innovation in exchange for royal sponsorship of his journey home aboard the Manila Galleon, which traditionally stopped in New Spain, a Spanish colonial territory. His proposal, however, attracted suspicion from Antonio Sebastián de Toledo Molina y Salazar, the viceroy of New Spain and Marquis of Mancera.

The viceroy questioned whether Muñoz possessed the scientific knowledge he claimed and worried that the friar was simply trying to persuade the king to pay for his travels. To test his abilities, Mancera presented him with the telescope and ordered him to examine it thoroughly. That assignment produced the technical description Moreno Madrid has now brought to light.

Determining whether Galileo actually manufactured the instrument is more complicated. Although the astronomer famously maintained that he had never sold a telescope and never intended to, very few instruments from his lifetime survive with reliable records of their origins. Of the eight surviving telescopes manufactured during the first half of the seventeenth century, none can be attributed to Galileo beyond dispute. Two preserved in the Museum of Florence have traditionally been credited to him, although that identification is not universally accepted. Galileo also left no technical analyses of his own telescopes.
There is, however, a possible connection between Galileo and the Spanish official who possessed Muñoz’s instrument.

Historical accounts indicate that Galileo presented three telescopes, one large and two smaller instruments, to Philip IV and his wife. He hoped to gain favor with the Spanish court and improve his chances of receiving a substantial reward offered for solving the “problem of longitude,” the longstanding difficulty of determining a ship’s east-west position while navigating at sea.

articles.title: Scientists Discover That Young Chimpanzees May Develop Accents Just Like Humans
articles.dek: The sounds animals make may carry clues to their social worlds, and young chimpanzees are helping scientists explore how communication takes shape beyond inherited biology.
paragraphs: The sounds animals make may carry clues to their social worlds, and young chimpanzees are helping scientists explore how communication takes shape beyond inherited biology.
Young chimpanzees may develop something resembling regional accents, with the sounds they make becoming increasingly different depending on the community in which they grow up.

Much like people who pick up subtle differences in speech from those around them, chimpanzees appear to develop population-specific vocal patterns as they mature. The finding challenges the long-held belief that their calls are largely fixed by genetics from birth.

A research team led by doctoral researcher Kassandra Giragosian from the School of Biological and Behavioural Sciences at Queen Mary University of London , in collaboration with the University of Portsmouth, compared the vocalizations of infant and juvenile chimpanzees from two geographically separated populations. By examining grunts, whimpers, and laughter, the researchers found that differences between the groups became more pronounced as the animals grew older.

Not all of these differences appeared at the same time. Some population-specific vocal characteristics were already detectable during infancy, while others emerged as the chimpanzees entered their juvenile years. This provides the first evidence that differences in chimpanzee vocalizations become increasingly distinct throughout early development.

“Understanding how communication develops during early life is fundamental to understanding animal behavior. Our findings show that chimpanzee vocalizations are not simply fixed from birth but continue to develop as young animals interact with their social and ecological environments,” says doctoral researcher Kassandra Giragosian.

Social interactions, environmental conditions, and other influences beyond genetics may therefore help shape how young chimpanzees communicate. Although the research does not establish precisely how these factors contribute to vocal development, the findings suggest that inherited traits alone cannot explain the differences between populations.

The discovery does not mean chimpanzees possess language or human-like speech, which involves an agreed vocabulary and grammar. Instead, it offers a new perspective on how communication develops in primates and how vocal patterns can differ between animal communities.

By examining communication at different stages of early life rather than simply comparing adults from different populations, the research provides a framework for investigating how communication systems emerge and diversify. It could also help scientists better understand the biological and environmental influences that shape vocal behavior across other species and the evolution of increasingly complex communication systems.

articles.title: Your Personality May Be Partly Written in Your DNA, Massive Study of 1 Million People Reveals
articles.dek: The personality traits others recognize in us may also have roots in our DNA, with research uncovering genetic connections that go beyond how we see ourselves.
paragraphs: The personality traits others recognize in us may also have roots in our DNA, with research uncovering genetic connections that go beyond how we see ourselves.

Could your DNA help explain why you are naturally outgoing, highly organized, or more prone to worrying than others? A large international study suggests that some of the personality traits that make us who we are may be partly rooted in our genes, raising a fascinating question about how much of our personality is determined before we are even born.

Researchers at the University of Tartu have identified more than 1,000 genetic variants associated with human personality in a study involving more than one million people. Published in the journal Nature , the findings offer new insight into how genetics contributes to differences in personality, while also showing why DNA alone cannot explain who we become.

The DNA of two randomly selected people is approximately 99. 9% identical. Differences in the remaining 0. 1% help influence characteristics such as appearance, disease risk, and responses to medication. The new research suggests that these small genetic differences are also associated with five major dimensions of personality: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism.

Scientists have known for decades that both genetics and life experiences influence personality. Finding the specific genetic differences involved has been much more difficult because personality is shaped by many genes, each contributing an extremely small effect. Detecting those subtle patterns requires enormous amounts of data.

Between 2021 and 2022, the Estonian Biobank gathered personality information from nearly 80,000 participants. Although substantial for Estonia, that sample was not large enough to reliably identify many of the genetic associations researchers were looking for.

The University of Tartu team therefore combined its findings with 45 other international datasets, creating a more geographically diverse study population. For certain personality traits, the researchers could analyze data from as many as 1. 1 million people. The Estonian sample was the third-largest of all participating groups and used the most comprehensive personality questionnaire.

The genetic associations were remarkably consistent across different populations, including people of varying ages and geographical backgrounds. However, the identified variants explained only about 4. 8% to 9. 3% of the differences in personality traits.

That relatively small proportion highlights how much remains unexplained. Social relationships, environmental influences, and personal experiences may all play substantial roles, along with the ways these factors interact with a person’s genetic makeup.

One particularly interesting feature of the Estonian research allowed scientists to examine personality from two perspectives. Participants could evaluate their own personalities and invite someone who knew them to provide an independent assessment.
“No other biobank in the world offers such an opportunity!” said Uku Vainik, Professor of Behavioral Genetics at the University of Tartu.

This approach helped researchers address an important question about personality research. Are genetic associations connected to characteristics that other people can actually observe, or do they mainly reflect how individuals think about themselves?
The researchers found substantial overlap between the genetic signals associated with self-reported personality traits and those identified through assessments by acquaintances.

“This shows that measurable personality traits are truly real, publicly observable characteristics of people, rather than merely individuals’ own opinions about themselves,” explained René Mõttus, Professor of Personality Psychology and co-lead of the study.

articles.title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang is getting his CEO job back, but history shows companies perform better when corporate boards take executive misbehavior seriously
articles.dek: The story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations.
paragraphs: The story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis.

This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the Nov. 12, 2026, ouster of its CEO , Jensen Huang, who remarkably returned to his job just 11 days later. But it actually transpired over 15 years ago at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd.

Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs – albeit in his case temporarily – over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is shifting from his behavior to his board – and the decisions that led to his exit.

Prominent industry leaders are questioning the board’s original decision to oust him. They include Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan – not to mention President Donald Trump , who reportedly directed the effort to get Huang reinstated.

As a scholar of management who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board had made the right call to force him out. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, I have repeatedly found that doing nothing, as a board, is worse than doing something.

CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization.

But it’s still hard for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. This is likely why the board chose to reinstate Jensen Huang. And why his return sets a terrible precedent.

One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct exit at a significantly higher rate than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because they’re forced out due to poor performance, my research shows.

One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who stepped down as chairman of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it.

Directors are also personally penalized for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may lose their board seats or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct may spill over to damage the reputations of those companies as well.
In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it.

In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of potential national security risks .

Another issue is moral hazard : when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation.

When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance is often even worse than the first.

Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while prompting criticism of the board for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991.

Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was recently ousted as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship.

In the case of Nvidia, Jensen reportedly lied to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future?
In reinstating him, the board said it “was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.”
Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake.

CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s often associated with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive.

Take Dov Charney’s tenure as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees.

It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U. S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. The board is likely looking at the totality of the issues and not just the personal misconduct.

In the runup to Huang’s return to Nvidia, the public debate had largely been centered on what the company might lose without Jensen Huang at the helm. An equally important question, though, is what the company and its board might risk by retaining a CEO whose conduct has raised serious questions about judgment, trust and organizational oversight.

The decision to reinstate him suggests that political pressure can interfere with companies’ hiring and firing for misconduct, and that powerful CEOs are above the normal corporate considerations that would lead to dismissal. The Nvidia case might set a precedent, as other CEOs and boards now know the playbook for getting away with misconduct.

articles.title: NASA Seeks Partners to Design First Nuclear Reactor for the Moon
articles.dek: NASA is seeking industry partners to develop and test the first nuclear reactor designed to provide electricity on the Moon, a major step toward establishing a sustained…
paragraphs: NASA is seeking industry partners to develop and test the first nuclear reactor designed to provide electricity on the Moon, a major step toward establishing a sustained human presence on the lunar surface.

Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1) will be a small fission power system that will generate 20 kilowatts of electricity, enough to power approximately 16 average U. S. households annually on Earth. For NASA’s plans for a Moon Base , that energy could support future habitats, communications systems, rovers, scientific instruments, and other essential infrastructure.
NASA aims to have a launch-ready system by 2030 and operate it on the Moon for at least five years after deployment.

Unlike solar power, which depends on sunlight, a nuclear reactor can generate electricity continuously, including during the Moon’s approximately two-week-long nights. This capability will enable future lunar operations, particularly in locations where sunlight is limited or unavailable.

“This request for proposals represents an important step forward as NASA partners with industry to establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface,” said Brian Giblin, NASA’s Lunar Reactor-1 program manager. “A reliable source of safe and abundant energy will be vital to future exploration of the lunar and Martian surface. Space nuclear systems will provide continuous power to NASA assets in any environment without dependency on sunlight.”

NASA’s Space Power and Reactor Capabilities Request for Proposals incorporates feedback received after the agency released a draft proposal in August and hosted an industry day in September at the Ohio Aerospace Institute in Cleveland. The solicitation requires that the reactor must meet Department of Energy (DOE) safety standards for nuclear operations.

While the primary purpose of the Request for Proposals is to advance the technology, testing, and flight design of LR-1, NASA may issue additional task orders to support the development of other space nuclear power systems. Proposals are due by Dec. 21.

Nuclear power will be increasingly important to NASA’s space exploration ambitions. Lunar nights last about 14 Earth days, while dust storms on Mars can block sunlight for months. Farther from the Sun, solar power becomes progressively less effective. Nuclear systems offer a reliable source of electricity in these challenging environments.

LR-1 is managed by the agency’s Space Reactors Division in partnership with the Department of Energy. The division is also responsible for the development of NASA’s Space Reactor‑1 (SR-1) Freedom. Scheduled to launch in 2028, SR-1 Freedom will deliver three SkyFall helicopters to Mars and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion, which uses electricity generated by a nuclear reactor to power spacecraft propulsion systems. This technology could enable future spacecraft to travel farther and undertake deep space missions that aren’t possible using conventional propulsion.

Together, LR-1 and SR-1 Freedom are advancing nuclear power and propulsion technologies to enable a new era of space exploration. By investing in these technologies, NASA and DOE are helping secure America’s leadership in space for decades to come.

articles.title: Pancreatic Cancer’s “Don’t Eat Me” Signal Reveals a Potential New Treatment Target
articles.dek: In preclinical experiments, drugs designed to fight pancreatic cancer also increased a protein that helps tumors survive, offering a possible clue to why treatment resistance…
paragraphs: In preclinical experiments, drugs designed to fight pancreatic cancer also increased a protein that helps tumors survive, offering a possible clue to why treatment resistance develops.

Pancreatic cancer has ways of protecting itself from the immune system, allowing tumor cells to survive when they might otherwise be destroyed. Researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center have identified a protein that appears to help tumors maintain this defense, and targeting it could make certain cancer treatments more effective.

The protein, called IL-18, normally helps regulate inflammation and the immune response. However, its levels are often elevated in people with pancreatic cancer, and higher levels have been linked to poorer outcomes. Scientists wanted to understand whether IL-18 was actively helping tumors grow or simply associated with more aggressive disease.

To investigate, they created genetically engineered models of pancreatic cancer with reduced IL-18 levels. Without as much of the protein, tumors grew more slowly, disease progression was delayed, and survival improved.

A closer examination of individual cells revealed a possible explanation. IL-18 increased levels of another protein called CD47, which acts as a “don’t eat me” signal. Cancer cells use this signal to avoid being destroyed by macrophages, immune cells that normally recognize and clear harmful or abnormal cells.

When IL-18 was reduced, macrophages became better at identifying and destroying tumor cells. The findings also suggest that IL-18 may influence how these immune cells enter tumors, remain there, or survive in the surrounding tissue, known as the tumor microenvironment.

The researchers also uncovered a potential connection to treatment resistance. Some promising pancreatic cancer drugs work by blocking KRAS, a protein that can drive cancer growth. Although these targeted therapies offer hope, some patients develop resistance.

In preclinical experiments, blocking KRAS increased IL-18 levels, potentially giving tumors another way to survive treatment. When researchers combined KRAS inhibition with reduced IL-18, the antitumor response improved, suggesting that targeting both proteins could be more effective than blocking KRAS alone.

The study, published in Gastroenterology , was co-led by Yang Chen, Ph. D. , assistant professor of Translational Molecular Pathology, and Xinlei Sun, Ph. D. , a postdoctoral fellow in the same department.

“Our results show that IL-18 helps pancreatic tumors stay hidden from the immune system and significantly contributes to disease progression and reduced survival,” Chen said. “Finding a way to safely target IL-18 in humans could have tremendous potential for enhancing the benefits of KRAS-targeted therapies and improving patient outcomes.”

The findings are still limited to preclinical research. Scientists will need to develop and test treatments that safely target IL-18 before determining whether combining them with KRAS inhibitors or other therapies can improve outcomes for people with pancreatic cancer.

articles.title: NASA+ Documentary Captures Europa Clipper’s Journey Into Deep Space
articles.dek: NASA invites the world behind the scenes to witness the story of Europa Clipper’s journey from a far-off vision to a cutting-edge deep space exploration mission with the…
paragraphs: NASA invites the world behind the scenes to witness the story of Europa Clipper’s journey from a far-off vision to a cutting-edge deep space exploration mission with the release of the agency’s newest documentary, “The Europa Concept.”
The documentary will air on NASA+ , the NASA app, and the agency’s website starting Monday, Nov. 23, and is coming soon to YouTube.

It took decades of science, thousands of dedicated minds, endless creativity, and a whole lot of grit to get the Europa Clipper spacecraft to the launch pad in 2024. Now the orbiter, the largest NASA has ever sent into deep space, is two years into its five-year, 1. 8 billion-mile (2. 9 billion-kilometer) journey to the Jupiter system, where it will conduct flybys of Europa in search of the conditions for life in the vast ocean thought to hide beneath the moon’s icy surface.

“The things we will learn from Europa Clipper will be so sensational, so fantastic, that everyone will be screaming for the next mission,” said Curt Niebur, program scientist in the Planetary Science Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “The only thing that matters is that we learn enough that we, in the broadest sense, want to do it again somewhere else — because that’s what exploration is.”

Following a team of dedicated engineers and scientists on their yearslong efforts, the documentary captures how they developed a mission to Europa and built a spacecraft capable of surviving one of the most punishing radiation environments in our solar system. A product of Jupiter’s powerful magnetic field, that same radiation may have contributed to creating a potentially habitable environment on Europa.

The moon, an object of fascination since its discovery by Galileo Galilei in 1610, only began to reveal its secrets with data obtained by NASA’s Pioneer 10 in 1973, followed the next year by Pioneer 11. But humanity didn’t get its first detailed look at Europa until Voyager 1’s flyby in 1979. More detailed glimpses of the moon followed from the agency’s Voyager 2, Galileo, Cassini, and Juno missions, each helping illuminate the way for Europa Clipper.

Work officially began on the mission at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California in 2013, initiating an 11-year trek to build the spacecraft and its suite of nine science instruments in time to launch during a specific period of planetary alignment. Along the way, the team encountered plenty of unforeseen challenges, including a global pandemic and, just before launch on Oct. 14, 2024, a Category 5 hurricane and tornadoes near NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

“With Europa Clipper, we’ve taken the next step in solar system exploration, which will help us uncover the mysteries of an ocean world, and ultimately, whether potentially habitable worlds beyond our own exist,” said Jordan Evans, director of flight projects at JPL and the mission’s previous project manager. “This documentary pays tribute to the ingenuity, teamwork, and dedication that continue to make this incredible mission possible.”

“The Europa Concept” takes audiences through the highs and lows alongside the thousands more who made Europa Clipper’s journey to the launch pad a success — and who will, in the coming years, be there to share the mission’s findings about humanity’s place in the cosmos.

Managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California, JPL leads the development of the Europa Clipper mission in partnership with the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, for NASA. The main spacecraft body was designed by APL in collaboration with JPL and NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, and NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia. The Planetary Missions Program Office at NASA Marshall executes program management of the Europa Clipper mission. NASA’s Launch Services Program, based at Kennedy, managed the launch service for the Europa Clipper spacecraft.

“With Europa Clipper, we’ve taken the next step in solar system exploration, which will help us uncover the mysteries of an ocean world, and ultimately, whether potentially habitable worlds beyond our own exist,” said Jordan Evans, director of flight projects at JPL and the mission’s previous project manager. “This documentary pays tribute to the ingenuity, teamwork, and dedication that continue to make this incredible mission possible.”

“The Europa Concept” takes audiences through the highs and lows alongside the thousands more who made Europa Clipper’s journey to the launch pad a success — and who will, in the coming years, be there to share the mission’s findings about humanity’s place in the cosmos.

Managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California, JPL leads the development of the Europa Clipper mission in partnership with the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, for NASA. The main spacecraft body was designed by APL in collaboration with JPL and NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, and NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia. The Planetary Missions Program Office at NASA Marshall executes program management of the Europa Clipper mission. NASA’s Launch Services Program, based at Kennedy, managed the launch service for the Europa Clipper spacecraft.

articles.title: NASA’s Webb Shows How Supernova Dust Chronicles Star Evolution
articles.dek: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has painted a vibrant tapestry of the legendary supernova remnant Cassiopeia A (Cas A).
paragraphs: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has painted a vibrant tapestry of the legendary supernova remnant Cassiopeia A (Cas A). Remnants like these are the clouds of gas and dust that remain following the explosion of a massive star and will eventually seed a new generation of stars and planets.

This high-resolution, mid-infrared observation from Webb reveals new details that are helping astronomers chronicle the structure and evolution of Cas A’s original star. The Webb data supports a scenario in which the interior of the star underwent a dramatic change, possibly just hours before its demise. These results published Monday in The Astrophysical Journal Letters .

Stars begin their lives as large clouds of mostly hydrogen gas and cosmic dust called molecular clouds. Eventually, gravity causes these molecular clouds to collapse, the material heats up, and protostars — infant stars — form. Under the constant pressure of gravity, hydrogen within a protostar begins to fuse into helium, which marks the point where protostars evolve into full-fledged stars like our Sun.

As hydrogen in the core runs out, the core contracts and heats until helium begins to fuse into heavier elements. This process repeats as stars like Cas A’s original star evolve, with increasingly heavier elements fusing in the core (eventually stopping at iron) and lighter elements fusing in surrounding layers. This leads to multiple shells of elements that provide a record of a star’s evolutionary history. When a star goes supernova, these elements are scattered into the surrounding space, where some of them condense to form dust grains, which can clump together.

By studying and mapping the composition of these individual, solar-system-sized dust clumps in Cas A, Webb found evidence of a shell merger, a process in which the layers inside a star mix before the explosion.

“Material within these shells churns and circulates, which can cause the shells to merge shortly before the supernova explosion,” said Tea Temim, lead author of the study and research scientist from Columbia University in New York. “So, for example, the oxygen- and carbon-burning shells in a star merge together and change the structure of the star significantly. And that would then change the chemical abundances that you would see after a supernova explosion in the ejecta of a supernova remnant.”

For the researchers to know where to look with Webb, they also leveraged data from NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope. Although it couldn’t resolve the minute details of the region during its observation , Spitzer identified three specific regions to observe with Webb’s keen eye.

Two of the targets were inside Cas A’s reverse-shocked region, where an inward-moving shock wave collides with debris thrown outward by the supernova. Webb observed that the ejecta in one of the two contained mostly silica dust, while the other was dominated by carbon dust. The third target was the “ Green Monster ,” a structure first discovered by Webb, which was found to be rich in complex magnesium silicates. Unlike the other two regions, the Green Monster originated from material the star shed before it exploded, rather than from the supernova’s ejecta.

Building on the X-ray observations of NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory and the JAXA-led XRISM , Webb mapped the dust composition of Cas A across the entire remnant, providing crucial insight into the shell merger phenomenon. Together, these observations indicate that the merger was underway very shortly before the supernova explosion.

“With Webb, the vast improvement in being able to resolve at the individual clump level helps us do more sophisticated dust chemistry,” said Dan Milisavljevic, associate professor and co-author of the study from Purdue University in West Lafayette, Indiana. “As a result, we can tie the explosion back to the makeup of the progenitor star hundreds of years afterward. It’s telling us about what was happening, we think, in the hours leading up to core collapse. Understanding this process is essential to explaining which elements the supernova explosion will release into the galaxy and how those elements enrich future generations of stars and planets.”

The dust map from Webb also reveals that the merger signatures are present throughout much of the supernova remnant. These efforts provide a new method for other astronomers who want to infer characteristics about an originating star’s structure by using the dust of a supernova remnant.
